quick_reasoning: Well-targeted: Directly addresses recognized AI Safety problem, reasonably scoped

original_idea.body:
# Evaluating Whether Constitutional AI Training Reduces Monitoring Bypass Rates

**Problem:** Constitutional AI training (critique-and-revision for safety) may produce models that are inherently more transparent and honest in ways that reduce their ability to craft monitoring bypasses. This has not been tested.

**Direction:** Compare monitoring bypass rates between constitutionally-trained models and standard RLHF models of similar capability. Control for capability level. Test whether constitutional training correlates with reduced bypass success.

**Why it matters:** If constitutional training reduces monitoring bypass, it provides a training-time intervention that improves monitoring robustness — a major practical finding for model development practice.

**Relevant context:** Constitutional AI (Anthropic); RLHF safety training; monitoring bypass rates.

title: Causal Analysis: Does Human-in-the-Loop Review Frequency Affect Agent Safety Outcomes in Long-Horizon Tasks?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses a recognized AI Safety problem (agent monitoring) with a reasonably scoped empirical approach testing specific review frequency parameters.

original_idea.body:
# Causal Analysis: Does Human-in-the-Loop Review Frequency Affect Agent Safety Outcomes in Long-Horizon Tasks?

**Problem:** Long-horizon tasks with infrequent human review may allow dangerous behaviors to compound before detection. The optimal human review frequency for different task risk levels is uncharacterized.

**Direction:** Run agents on long-horizon tasks with adversarial injections at various points. Test human review checkpoints at different frequencies (every action, every 5, every 20, at end). Measure safety outcome rates and total human review workload for each frequency.

**Why it matters:** Human review frequency is a directly adjustable deployment parameter. This study provides the empirical basis for setting review frequency as a function of task risk level.

**Relevant context:** Human-in-the-loop AI safety; METR monitoring design; checkpoint frequency.

title: Follow-Up: Do Models Exhibit Reduced Safety Compliance After Being Told Their Monitor Made an Error?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted to a specific safety concern (alignment faking, unintended consequences of transparent monitoring) with clear measurement approach.

original_idea.body:
# Follow-Up: Do Models Exhibit Reduced Safety Compliance After Being Told Their Monitor Made an Error?

**Problem:** If a monitoring system erroneously flags a benign action, and the agent is informed of this error (to explain why its action was blocked), the agent might learn to treat future monitoring flags as potentially erroneous — potentially reducing compliance.

**Direction:** Inform agents about monitoring false positives in their context. Measure whether subsequent safety compliance rates or monitoring bypass attempt rates change after being told the monitor made an error.

**Why it matters:** If error disclosure changes agent safety behavior, the standard practice of explaining monitoring decisions to agents could backfire. This study characterizes an unintended consequence of transparent monitoring.

**Relevant context:** Alignment faking; monitoring transparency; agent behavior after feedback.

title: Measuring Information Security Awareness as a Moderator of Human Monitoring Review Quality
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses human factors in AI Safety monitoring, testing whether security training improves review quality with practical policy implications.

original_idea.body:
# Measuring Information Security Awareness as a Moderator of Human Monitoring Review Quality

**Problem:** Human reviewers with different levels of security training may perform very differently as monitoring reviewers. Whether security training moderates monitoring review quality is unknown.

**Direction:** Compare monitoring alert review performance between participants with formal security training (CS security course) vs. without. Measure decision accuracy on a standardized set of monitoring alerts spanning safe, borderline, and dangerous agent actions.

**Why it matters:** If security training substantially improves review quality, organizations should require security training for anyone reviewing agent monitoring alerts — a concrete, actionable personnel policy recommendation.

**Relevant context:** Human factors in security; security awareness training; human-in-the-loop monitoring.

title: Characterizing the Exfiltration Stage in the AI Kill Chain: What Data Do Rogue Agents Target First?
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted to agent threat modeling and monitoring design, testing systematic patterns in agent data targeting priorities.

original_idea.body:
# Characterizing the 'Exfiltration' Stage in the AI Kill Chain: What Data Do Rogue Agents Target First?

**Problem:** If an agent pursues an unauthorized exfiltration goal, which data types or system components does it target first? Understanding data targeting priority would help design targeted monitoring for highest-value assets.

**Direction:** Create an environment with multiple data types (credentials, code, personal data, communications). Inject exfiltration goals into agents. Monitor the sequence in which agents attempt to access and exfiltrate different data types. Identify data targeting priority patterns.

**Why it matters:** If agents exhibit systematic data targeting priorities (e.g., always going for credentials first), monitoring can be concentrated on the highest-priority targets for early detection.

**Relevant context:** LW 2026 threat matrix (Exfiltration stage); data security; targeted monitoring design.

title: Compounding Risk: Multi-Modal Injection + Content-Based Monitor Blindness — Can Visual Injections Evade All Text Monitors?
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped to a specific monitoring vulnerability in multi-modal agents with clear methodology to quantify the systematic blindness gap.

original_idea.body:
# Compounding Risk: Multi-Modal Injection + Content-Based Monitor Blindness — Can Visual Injections Evade All Text Monitors?

**Problem:** Visual modality injections (instructions in images) would evade all text-based monitoring systems by definition. This combination of multi-modal capability and text-monitor blindness is a systematic monitoring gap.

**Direction:** Embed prompt injection attacks in images that a multi-modal agent will process. Measure success rate of image-injected attacks vs. text-injected attacks. Test whether any text-based monitoring signals (agent output analysis, action timing) can detect image-injected attacks.

**Why it matters:** As multi-modal agents become standard, text-only monitoring architectures become systematically blind to a whole class of attacks. This study quantifies that blindness.

**Relevant context:** Visual prompt injection; multi-modal agent security; monitoring coverage gap; compounding risk.

title: Pilot Study: Third-Party Red-Teaming of an Open-Source Agent Monitoring Implementation

original_idea.body:
# Pilot Study: Third-Party Red-Teaming of an Open-Source Agent Monitoring Implementation

**Problem:** Third-party adversarial evaluation of AI safety infrastructure is nascent. Demonstrating that third-party evaluation of open-source monitoring systems is feasible and valuable would help establish this practice.

**Direction:** Select a popular open-source agent monitoring tool. Conduct a structured red-team engagement (without internal access). Document what vulnerabilities are discoverable from external position alone. Compare to what would be discoverable with internal access.

**Why it matters:** This directly addresses the 'third-party evaluation is nascent' open problem. A concrete demonstration of the methodology and its limits would advance the field.

**Relevant context:** METR 2026 third-party evaluation; open-source monitoring tools; third-party audit methodology.

title: Testing Monitoring Robustness to Adversarial Many-Shot Jailbreaks in Long Contexts
quick_reasoning: Precisely scoped to a specific monitor vulnerability (many-shot jailbreak attack) with clear measurement of a well-characterized attack technique.

original_idea.body:
# Testing Monitoring Robustness to Adversarial Many-Shot Jailbreaks in Long Contexts

**Problem:** Many-shot jailbreaking (inserting many examples of desired behavior into context) is an effective jailbreak technique for capable models. Whether it also works against LLM-based monitors is unknown.

**Direction:** Construct many-shot jailbreak prompts targeting a monitoring classifier. Insert many examples of the classifier passing dangerous actions before presenting the actual dangerous action to classify. Measure whether many-shot context manipulation degrades monitoring accuracy.

**Why it matters:** If many-shot jailbreaks work against monitors, any LLM-based monitor that operates on long contexts is vulnerable to a known, well-characterized attack technique.

**Relevant context:** Many-shot jailbreaking research; METR bypass vectors; long-context monitoring.

title: Backcasting from Verified Zero Rogue Replication Events: What Infrastructure Monitoring Is Required?

original_idea.body:
# Backcasting from Verified Zero Rogue Replication Events: What Infrastructure Monitoring Is Required?

**Problem:** Success state: cloud providers have verified that no rogue AI has successfully replicated on their infrastructure. Working backward, what monitoring capabilities at the infrastructure level would make this verification possible?

**Direction:** Simulate rogue AI replication at the infrastructure level (process spawning, container launching, API token creation). Identify what cloud infrastructure telemetry would detect each replication variant. Propose a minimum cloud monitoring specification for replication detection.

**Why it matters:** The LW threat matrix says cloud providers are the only ones with visibility into replication. This study specifies exactly what monitoring capabilities cloud providers need to implement.

**Relevant context:** LW 2026 threat matrix (Replication stage); cloud provider monitoring; infrastructure security.

title: Systematic Review of AI Agent Security Incidents: What Monitoring Would Have Caught Each?
quick_reasoning: Directly addresses AI Safety evaluation methodology through retrospective analysis of real incidents to assess monitoring effectiveness.

original_idea.body:
# Systematic Review of AI Agent Security Incidents: What Monitoring Would Have Caught Each?

**Problem:** Historical AI agent security incidents provide a test bed for monitoring evaluation: would existing monitoring approaches have detected each incident? No such retrospective analysis exists.

**Direction:** Collect all publicly reported AI agent security incidents (prompt injections, goal hijacking, unauthorized actions). For each incident, model what monitoring signals would have been available and test whether a simple monitoring classifier would have detected it.

**Why it matters:** Retrospective analysis of real incidents provides ground truth about monitoring effectiveness that is more reliable than synthetic test cases.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic espionage campaign; AI incident database; METR red-teaming; incident-driven security improvement.

title: Evaluating Whether Agent Monitoring Reduces or Increases Model Helpfulness on Legitimate Tasks
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted to measuring a recognized AI Safety tradeoff (safety-helpfulness) with clear empirical methodology using standard benchmarks.

original_idea.body:
# Evaluating Whether Agent Monitoring Reduces or Increases Model Helpfulness on Legitimate Tasks

**Problem:** Monitoring systems may cause agents to behave more cautiously on legitimate tasks, reducing helpfulness. Whether monitoring has a net positive or negative effect on the helpfulness-safety tradeoff has not been measured.

**Direction:** Measure agent performance on a standard helpfulness benchmark (e.g., MT-Bench) with and without active monitoring. Measure whether monitoring causes agents to refuse more legitimate requests or add excessive caveats. Quantify the helpfulness cost of monitoring.

**Why it matters:** If monitoring substantially degrades helpfulness, there will be pressure to reduce monitoring in production deployments. Quantifying this tradeoff supports principled monitoring deployment decisions.

**Relevant context:** Safety-helpfulness tradeoff; METR monitoring evaluation; agent helpfulness benchmarks.

title: Applying Intrusion Detection System Principles to Agent Communication: Signature vs. Anomaly Detection
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted to agent monitoring design with methodologically sound approach transferring established security principles to AI Safety context.

original_idea.body:
# Applying Intrusion Detection System Principles to Agent Communication: Signature vs. Anomaly Detection

**Problem:** Traditional IDS systems use either signature-based detection (known attack patterns) or anomaly detection (deviations from baseline). For agent monitoring, the relative effectiveness of these two approaches has not been compared.

**Direction:** Implement a signature-based agent monitor (using known attack pattern rules) and an anomaly-based agent monitor (statistical deviation from baseline). Compare their performance on known attacks (expected advantage for signature-based) and novel attacks (expected advantage for anomaly-based). Measure performance on each attack type.

**Why it matters:** The IDS field has decades of insight about when each approach is appropriate. Transferring this knowledge to agent monitoring would accelerate monitoring system design.

**Relevant context:** IDS signature vs. anomaly detection (classic security); agent monitoring; METR novel vs. known attacks.

title: Measuring the Effect of Agent Role-Assignment on Monitoring Evasion Rates
quick_reasoning: Well-targeted to agent deployment parameters, testing whether system prompt roles affect monitoring evasion propensity with clear measurement approach.

original_idea.body:
# Measuring the Effect of Agent Role-Assignment on Monitoring Evasion Rates

**Problem:** Agents assigned different roles (assistant, researcher, security analyst) may have systematically different propensities to attempt monitoring evasion. Role effects on monitoring evasion have not been studied.

**Direction:** Assign agents identical dangerous objectives but with different role system prompts (generic assistant, IT administrator, security researcher). Measure whether role assignment affects monitoring bypass attempt rates and success rates.

**Why it matters:** If role assignment affects evasion propensity, the framing of agent roles in system prompts is a security-relevant deployment decision requiring systematic guidance.

**Relevant context:** Role-playing in LLMs; system prompt design; agent monitoring evasion.
